opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. You know, there's this idea that people often find surprising, which goes back to Hans Moravec in the 1980s: the things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or doing calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, and the things that are easy for us, things a two-year-old can do, like picking up a cup or stacking blocks, turn out to be incredibly hard for robots. That's Moravec's paradox, and I think it's still very much with us.

The reason comes down to physics. When a robot reaches out to grasp an object, say a pen on a table, it has to deal with an enormous amount of uncertainty. Its cameras can't perfectly perceive where the object is or exactly what shape it is. Its motors and joints aren't perfectly precise, so its hand doesn't end up exactly where it's commanded. And then there's the contact itself, which is the really subtle part. Friction is extremely hard to model. Tiny variations in surface texture, in the distribution of mass inside the object, or in where the fingertip makes contact can completely change the outcome. The pen might roll, or slip, or pivot in a way that's essentially unpredictable. These are what we'd call chaotic or highly sensitive dynamics. Microscopic differences at the moment of contact lead to macroscopic differences in what happens next.

Humans handle this effortlessly, and we don't even notice we're doing it. We have this incredibly rich sense of touch, and millions of years of evolution have tuned our hands and nervous systems to compensate for uncertainty in real time. Robots don't have anything close to that yet.

That's why I push back a bit on the current excitement. There's a lot of enthusiasm right now, partly driven by the success of large language models, that if we just collect enough data and train big enough models, robots will suddenly be able to do everything: fold laundry, clean your house, cook dinner. And I understand the appeal. But language models had the benefit of the entire internet, essentially trillions of tokens of text. For robot manipulation we don't have anything like that. Some estimates suggest it would take tens of thousands of years of robot experience to match the scale of data that language models were trained on. And you can't just scrape it from the web, because videos of people doing things don't contain the forces, the torques, the tactile feedback that a robot actually needs.

So I see manipulation as a fundamental challenge because it sits right at the intersection of perception, control, and physics, and the physics part is genuinely difficult. It's not just an engineering problem we haven't gotten around to. My view is that we'll make real progress, but it will come from combining approaches: good old-fashioned engineering, analytic models of physics, and simulation, together with data-driven learning, rather than expecting any one of them to solve it alone. And I think we should be honest with the public about the timelines, because overpromising has hurt this field before.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing people often miss is that manipulation looks easy because we do it effortlessly. You reach into a cluttered drawer, you grab a pair of scissors, you don't think about it. But what's actually happening physically is extraordinarily complex. You've got friction, which is notoriously hard to model. You've got contact mechanics, where tiny variations in the surface, a bit of oil on your finger, a slightly different angle, completely change whether the object slips or stays. And you've got uncertainty about the object itself: its mass distribution, its exact shape, where it's sitting relative to your hand.

In my lab we've spent years on grasping, and what we found is that even for a single rigid object, predicting whether a grasp will succeed is a genuinely hard problem. There's this gap between how clean the physics looks on paper, the equations for a two-fingered grasp, and how messy it is in practice. Small errors in perception and control compound, and the real world doesn't give you a second chance when a glass tips over.

And that's just picking things up. Then you get into deformable objects, cables, cloth, bags, food. A bag of chips doesn't have a fixed shape. Every time you touch it, it changes. The configuration space is essentially infinite. We can't even write down the state of the system the way we can for a chess board or a robot arm's joint angles.

So I like to point to what's sometimes called Moravec's paradox: the things that are hardest for humans, like playing Go or doing calculus, turn out to be relatively tractable for machines, while the things a toddler does, picking up a toy and putting it in a box, remain very difficult. I think that's because manipulation isn't really an information problem. It's a physical problem, where you're interacting with a world that pushes back, and the data you need is often only available through contact itself. That's why I see it as fundamental. Until we make real progress there, robots will stay confined to the structured environments of factories, and the vision of a robot helping in your home or a hospital remains out of reach.

astra-6.text:
Well, think about picking up a coffee cup. It seems almost effortless to us, but the robot has to work out where to grasp it, how much force to apply, and what will happen when it lifts. Is the surface slippery? Is the cup full? Is the handle fragile? The image alone doesn’t tell you all of that.

And contact is where things get particularly difficult. Small differences in position or friction can mean the difference between a stable grasp and the object slipping. If you’re handling a shirt or a cable, the object itself changes shape as you manipulate it. So you’re not just trying to recognise the world; you’re trying to predict how it will respond to your actions, with incomplete information.

Humans are remarkably good at this. We feel something start to slip and adjust our grip without consciously thinking about it. Getting a robot to combine perception, touch, and action in that way, across the enormous variety of everyday objects, is a fundamental challenge. You can engineer a system to repeat one motion very reliably. It’s much harder to make it handle something it hasn’t encountered before.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’re manipulating an everyday object, you’re making contact with the world, and that contact is surprisingly difficult to model. Think about picking up a set of keys or a shirt. You have friction, you have objects sliding against one another, and in the case of the shirt, the shape changes as you touch it. Small differences in where you make contact can produce very different outcomes.

And you don’t know all the relevant properties in advance. You may not know how heavy an object is, where its center of mass lies, or how slippery its surface is. So a robot has to act with incomplete information, then use what happens to decide what to do next.

Humans make this look effortless. We adjust our grip almost without thinking. But getting a robot to do that reliably across a wide variety of objects forces us to confront both the complexity of the physics and the uncertainty in our models. That’s what makes manipulation such a fundamental challenge.
